Unfair baseline comparison: prompt-only models have zero domain exposure; no serious attempt to improve prompt-based approaches (better prompts, retrieval-augmentation, etc.)
No human evaluation of synthesized reasoning quality, coherence, or impact on interpretability
Small test set (932 cases, ~2.9% of data) without confidence intervals or significance testing; no per-action-type error breakdown
Limited novelty: core finding (fine-tuning and reasoning help) is expected; contribution is mainly application to action generation task

strengths: Clear motivation distinguishing objective accuracy from subjective believability in behavior simulation
Large-scale real-world dataset (31,865 sessions, 230,965 actions) from production e-commerce platform
Comprehensive evaluation of multiple SOTA LLMs (Claude, Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen) in both prompt-only and fine-tuned settings
Methodologically sound with proper train/test splits avoiding user overlap and ablation studies demonstrating reasoning importance
Systematic task formulation with clear definitions of context, reasoning, and action components
Demonstrates substantial improvement from fine-tuning (17.26% vs 11.86%) with actionable insights for practitioners
Well-written paper with effective visualizations showing fine-tuned models better match human action distributions
Honest acknowledgment of limitations in Section 6 regarding scope, reasoning validation, and action space
weaknesses: Single-task evaluation limited to online shopping severely restricts generalizability claims; no evidence findings transfer to other behavior simulation tasks (social interactions, UI testing, trust modeling)

Core contribution undermined by unvalidated synthesized reasoning traces: authors explicitly acknowledge 'we have not evaluated on real human-annotated datasets containing authentic reasoning traces'—this is critical since reasoning improvement is a main claim
No human evaluation of reasoning quality despite reasoning being a key contribution; authors admit 'we did not conduct human evaluations on interpretability and usefulness of generated reasoning'
Very low absolute accuracy (17.26%) raises questions about practical utility; no discussion of whether this suffices for real-world deployment or impact on downstream applications
Missing comparisons with non-LLM baselines (RNNs, Transformers, traditional behavior models); unclear if improvements stem from LLM-specific capabilities or just fine-tuning benefits
No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance analysis; single-run results without reliability assessment
Oversimplified action space (only 3 actions: click, type_and_submit, terminate) omits scrolling, hovering, waiting—may not capture realistic user behavior
Limited error analysis and failure mode investigation; no categorization of difficult action types or root cause analysis of errors
Dataset source anonymized and reproducibility unclear; no mention of release plans
Small test set (932 cases) with unclear construction; single epoch training without convergence analysis

strengths: Makes a valuable distinction between subjective 'believability' and objective 'accuracy' in behavior simulation, addressing an important methodological gap in prior work
Leverages a substantial real-world dataset (31,865 sessions, 230,965 actions) from an e-commerce platform, providing a meaningful resource for reproducible research
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple SOTA models (Claude, DeepSeek-R1, Llama, Qwen, Mistral) in both prompt-only and fine-tuned settings with statistical significance testing
Clear empirical evidence that fine-tuning improves action accuracy by 5.4% and outcome prediction F1 by 13.98% compared to prompt-only methods
Provides actionable error analysis (Figure 3) revealing systematic failure modes, such as ICL models over-generating purchases and struggling with termination decisions
Well-justified design choices for context representation (simplified HTML with hierarchical element naming) that prioritize adaptability and LLM familiarity
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—fine-tuning LLMs on domain data and auxiliary task supervision are standard techniques; the contribution is primarily empirical rather than algorithmic

Critical flaw: synthesized reasoning traces are generated by Claude 3.5 Sonnet but never validated against human reasoning; no human evaluation of whether synthesized reasoning aligns with actual user thinking, making it unclear whether improvements stem from genuine reasoning patterns or artificial auxiliary supervision

Severe scope limitation: evaluation restricted to a single online shopping domain from one e-commerce platform; no evidence that findings generalize to other tasks (web navigation, social interaction, UX testing) despite motivating multiple domains

Statistical rigor issues: test set of 357 sessions (932 cases) is small; sequential actions within sessions are not independent yet treated as separate test cases, violating independence assumptions; no cross-validation, confidence intervals, or multiple runs

Questionable ground truth: models trained to generate synthesized reasoning from LLM-generated examples creates compounding bias risk; if Claude's reasoning contains systematic biases, trained models learn those biases rather than authentic human patterns

Evaluation lacks human assessment: no human judgment of whether generated behaviors appear realistic, and no validation that reasoning explanations are coherent or informative to humans despite claiming to enhance interpretability

Reproducibility concerns: dataset likely non-releasable due to commercial sensitivity (not addressed); no code provided; limited hyperparameter details beyond training setup, preventing independent reproduction

Missing critical comparisons: no ablation on context representation choices, no comparison with other behavior modeling approaches, no domain-specific baselines; limited analysis of what patterns fine-tuned models actually learn

Metric limitations: exact match accuracy for actions is uninformed about error severity (clicking wrong vs. right button treated equally); binary F1 for outcomes is limited; exact match doesn't account for behavioral similarity or partial correctness relevant to simulation

Presentation and framing: title 'Prompting is Not All You Need!' is catchy but misleading—prompting may suffice for believability even if not accuracy; this critical distinction should be prominent; limited qualitative analysis with no example action sequences shown

strengths: Addresses important gap between subjective 'believability' and objective 'accuracy' in LLM behavior simulation, filling a clear evaluation gap in prior work
Large-scale real-world dataset (31,865 sessions, 230,965 actions) from actual e-commerce platform is significantly more credible than synthetic benchmarks
Process-centric, action-level evaluation is more rigorous than prior work focusing only on final task outcomes
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple SOTA models (Llama, Claude, DeepSeek-R1, Mistral, Qwen) in both in-context learning and fine-tuning settings
Thorough empirical analysis including ablation studies, error categorization, action distribution visualization, and statistical significance testing
Clear findings with strong empirical support: out-of-the-box LLMs achieve ~12% accuracy; fine-tuning improves to ~17%; synthesized reasoning provides further gains
Well-motivated methodology: simplified HTML representation is justified; hierarchical naming practical; reasoning synthesis approach with think-aloud examples is sensible
Actionable insights about behavioral misalignment, including observation that models over-complete vs. under-terminate compared to humans
weaknesses: Limited to single domain (online shopping) and single e-commerce platform; generalizability to other behavior simulation tasks (social interaction, trust games, UI/UX testing) completely unknown, undermining broad claims about LLM agents
Synthetic reasoning traces generated by Claude 3.5 Sonnet are not validated against human reasoning; no human evaluation provided; high risk of introducing model bias into training data
Modest absolute performance (17.26% best action accuracy, 33.86% best F1) raises serious questions about practical applicability; unclear if these results are sufficient for real applications
Small test set of 357 sessions with 932 test cases relative to 230k+ actions dataset; no confidence intervals reported, only p-values; concerns about result stability

Incomplete investigation of why prompting fails; hypothesis about task completion bias mentioned but not rigorously tested; missing ablations on context adequacy, training objectives, or context length
Reproducibility severely limited: proprietary dataset cannot be released, platform identity withheld, no code or model release mentioned—critically limiting for a benchmarking paper
Limited technical novelty: core contribution is standard supervised fine-tuning; reasoning synthesis uses existing LLMs; main novelty is evaluation rather than methodology

Mechanisms of reasoning improvements unclear: is benefit from more training signal or actual reasoning? Inconsistent ablation results (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B: 15.77%→9.31% vs. 1B: 7.53%→11.13%) unexplained
Action space oversimplified (click, type_and_submit, terminate only); missing scrolling, hovering, waiting; may not reflect realistic web interaction
Missing baselines: no comparison to non-LLM approaches (Markov chains, behavior cloning, frequency models); cannot contextualize whether 17% is good/bad
Evaluation metric uses strict exact-match with no partial credit; could mask cases where models generate semantically similar but syntactically different actions
Training/test split not clearly specified; unclear how 31,865 sessions divided or whether stratified; affects reproducibility and validity
Limited exploration of practical applications; UI/UX testing mentioned but not deeply developed; unclear deployment scenarios
